subject: mcc-acute-care
title: DKA and HHS: Recognition and Initial Management

steps.tx: **Diabetic ketoacidosis** (DKA) is defined by hyperglycaemia, ketosis and metabolic acidosis, usually in type 1 diabetes. **Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state** (HHS) shows marked hyperglycaemia and high effective osmolality with little or no ketoacidosis, typically in older type 2 patients. Both are emergencies driven by relative insulin deficiency with raised counter-regulatory hormones. Recognising which one you face decides the fluids and insulin plan.
steps.say: Diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA, is defined by high blood glucose, ketones in the blood or urine, and metabolic acidosis, and it usually occurs in type 1 diabetes. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, or HHS, shows marked hyperglycaemia and high effective osmolality with little or no ketoacidosis, and it typically affects older people with type 2 diabetes. Both are emergencies caused by relative insulin deficiency together with raised counter-regulatory hormones. Recognising which one you face decides the fluids and insulin plan.

Can be altered in severe cases

steps.tx: In DKA, **bicarbonate** falls and the **anion gap** widens because **ketoacids** accumulate. Severity is graded by the **arterial pH** and the **serum bicarbonate**, with reduced consciousness marking the most serious end of the spectrum. Check **serum potassium** before starting insulin, because total body potassium is depleted even when the measured level appears normal.
steps.say: In diabetic ketoacidosis, bicarbonate drops and the anion gap gets wider, since ketoacids build up in the blood. Severity is judged from arterial pH and serum bicarbonate together, and a reduced level of consciousness signals the most serious end of the spectrum. Before insulin is started, serum potassium needs checking. Total body potassium is depleted even when the measured level looks normal, so insulin can drive it dangerously low if this is missed.

nodes.label: Grade severity by pH and bicarbonate

steps.tx: Euglycaemic DKA occurs with **SGLT2 inhibitors** such as empagliflozin, especially with poor intake, vomiting or surgery. Glucose may be only 11 mmol/L despite high ketones and acidosis. Treatment still needs fluids and insulin, but **dextrose** must run alongside insulin to prevent hypoglycaemia while ketogenesis is suppressed. Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and check for precipitating causes such as sepsis or infection.
steps.say: Euglycaemic DKA occurs with SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin, especially with poor intake, vomiting or surgery. Glucose may be only 11 millimoles per litre despite high ketones and acidosis. Treatment still needs fluids and insulin, but dextrose must run alongside insulin to prevent hypoglycaemia while ketogenesis is suppressed. Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and look for precipitating causes such as sepsis or infection.

steps.tx: In HHS, the **effective serum osmolality** is high, and altered consciousness is common. Free water deficit is corrected gradually after initial isotonic saline, because rapid lowering of osmolality risks cerebral oedema. Watch sodium and glucose closely. Metformin-associated risk is relevant if the patient is on metformin with dehydration or renal impairment, and metformin should be withheld during acute illness.
